## Intellectual Merit

This project will develop a unified statistical framework for **zero-inflated penalized beta regression**, addressing a methodological gap at the intersection of bounded-data modeling, zero inflation, and high-dimensional regression. Beta regression provides a natural framework for continuous outcomes restricted to the unit interval, but standard beta models cannot directly accommodate observations at zero. Conversely, methods for zero-inflated outcomes often do not fully exploit the continuous bounded structure of the positive observations. These limitations become particularly important when the number of potential predictors is large relative to the available sample size, when predictors are highly correlated, or when the scientific objective requires simultaneous modeling of the probability of a structural zero and the magnitude of a positive outcome.

The central intellectual contribution of the proposed research is the development of penalized estimation and inference for a zero-inflated beta regression model in which the mechanisms governing zero occurrence and the distribution of positive outcomes can be modeled jointly. The project will investigate how regularization can be incorporated into both components of the model while preserving the distinct statistical interpretations of the zero-generating and continuous processes. Particular attention will be given to the consequences of penalization for estimation, variable selection, prediction, and interpretation when the two model components share predictors or contain overlapping but distinct sets of covariates.

A major component of the project will be the development of the theoretical foundations of the proposed methodology. The research will characterize the statistical properties of penalized estimators under relevant asymptotic regimes and will investigate conditions under which the proposed procedures achieve consistent estimation and meaningful variable-selection behavior. The project will examine the effects of zero inflation, dispersion, predictor dimensionality, and dependence among covariates on estimator performance. These results will clarify when penalization provides useful regularization and when the additional complexity introduced by zero inflation creates challenges for estimation and inference.

The project will also address computational and inferential challenges that arise from the proposed model. Penalized likelihood optimization for a two-component zero-inflated model can produce a nontrivial computational problem because parameters associated with the zero and positive components may be strongly coupled. The research will develop efficient estimation algorithms and investigate their numerical stability across a range of sample sizes, degrees of zero inflation, and predictor dimensions. Resampling and other inferential procedures will be studied to provide practical uncertainty quantification for regression parameters and scientifically relevant functions of those parameters.

Simulation studies will be used to establish the finite-sample behavior of the proposed methods and to identify conditions under which existing approaches perform poorly. Comparisons will consider both statistical performance and practical criteria, including estimation error, prediction accuracy, variable-selection properties, calibration, computational cost, and robustness to model misspecification. Particular emphasis will be placed on distinguishing failures caused by ignoring zero inflation from failures caused by ignoring the bounded nature of the positive observations. This will provide a systematic assessment of the circumstances in which the proposed methodology offers advantages over existing regression strategies.

An important aspect of the research is the development of diagnostics and model-assessment procedures. A flexible model is useful only if investigators can determine whether its assumptions are reasonable for their data. The project will therefore investigate residual diagnostics, assessment of the zero-generating component, sensitivity to influential observations, and methods for evaluating the adequacy of the beta component. These tools will help distinguish genuine evidence for a zero-inflated mechanism from apparent zero inflation arising from model misspecification or other features of the data.

The methodological developments will be accompanied by open-source computational implementations and reproducible research materials. The resulting software will provide researchers with accessible implementations of the proposed estimation, variable-selection, inference, and diagnostic procedures. Simulation code and examples will allow researchers to evaluate the methods under conditions relevant to their own applications. This computational component is an integral part of the intellectual contribution because it will translate the theoretical developments into procedures that can be independently evaluated and extended.

The proposed research is expected to advance statistical methodology in three related ways. First, it will extend beta regression to settings in which excess zeros and high-dimensional predictor structures occur simultaneously. Second, it will establish theoretical and computational foundations for penalization in a multi-component bounded-outcome model. Third, it will develop inferential and diagnostic tools that connect the resulting methodology to practical statistical analysis. Together, these contributions will provide a more complete framework for regression with zero-inflated bounded continuous outcomes and establish a foundation for further work on regularized models for constrained response variables.
